title: Irish soda bread
subtitle: Quick buttermilk loaf with a tender crumb
excerpt: A soft, dense loaf made with wholemeal flour and buttermilk, leavened entirely by bicarbonate of soda reacting with the acid in the milk. Ready in under an hour, no yeast, no proving.
sourceNotes: Traditional Irish farmhouse bread. The recipe appears in variant forms across 19th-century Irish domestic cookery manuscripts. The bicarbonate-of-soda method became standard from the 1840s when reliable baking soda reached rural Ireland.

recipe.yieldDescription: one 20 cm round loaf, serves 6 to 8
recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, wrap tightly in cling film, and freeze for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature and warm briefly in the oven before serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles easily. Bake two loaves side by side. The method is forgiving and consistent.

content.text: Soda bread is a quick loaf leavened with bicarbonate of soda and buttermilk rather than yeast. It has a dense, tender crumb and a slightly tangy flavour, and it goes from flour to oven in under 10 minutes. The crust cracks along the scored cross as it bakes.

The main thing to get right is not overworking the dough. Mix briefly, shape quickly, and get it in the oven before the leavening reaction slows. A light hand makes a much better loaf than a thorough one.

items.prepNote: shaken; use soured milk if unavailable

content.text: If you cannot find buttermilk, add a tablespoon of lemon juice to 400 ml of whole milk, stir, and leave for 5 minutes until it curdles slightly. It works as well as commercial buttermilk.
Heat the oven to 200°C fan (220°C conventional). Dust a baking tray with flour.
Put both flours, the bicarbonate of soda, and the salt into a large bowl. Mix briefly with your fingers.

Make a well in the centre. Pour in the buttermilk. Use a wooden spoon or your hand to bring the dough together. Work quickly: as soon as the dough comes away from the sides of the bowl, stop mixing. Overworked dough makes a tight loaf.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Shape it into a round about 20 cm across. It will be slightly sticky; that is correct. Set it on the prepared tray.
Cut a deep cross through the loaf, almost to the base. This lets heat reach the centre and gives you the classic four-section crack.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until the crust is deep brown and the loaf sounds hollow when you knock the base with your knuckles.
Wrap the hot loaf in a clean tea towel and leave it to rest for 15 minutes. The steam softens the crust slightly and finishes the crumb.

items.symptom: The loaf is dense and heavy
items.cause: The dough was overworked or the oven was not hot enough
items.fix: Mix only until the dough just comes together. Check your oven temperature with a thermometer.

items.symptom: The loaf has a pale, gummy centre
items.cause: Underbaked; the internal temperature did not reach 95°C
items.fix: Return to the oven for 5 to 10 minutes. The hollow-tap test is reliable: a properly baked loaf sounds clearly hollow.
Wrap the hot loaf in a damp tea towel for 10 minutes. The steam softens the crust considerably.

items.symptom: The loaf spread flat instead of holding its shape
items.cause: Too much buttermilk or the dough was too wet
items.fix: Use the smaller end of the buttermilk range and add liquid gradually until the dough just holds together.

content.text: Soda bread is the bread of the Irish farmhouse kitchen. Bicarbonate of soda arrived in rural Ireland in the 1840s, and the combination with buttermilk, the byproduct of churning, gave home cooks a loaf that needed neither a starter culture nor a proving drawer. It became the everyday bread of a country that had no baking tradition of yeasted loaves.
Eat it fresh, within a few hours of baking. The crumb softens overnight and it is at its best toasted from the second day onwards. Good with butter and a scraping of jam, or with soup.
